533.title: Feed my sheep (John 21:15–25)
533.hook: three questions for Peter, and a closing line: the world could not hold all the books
533.tomorrow: To the ends of the earth
533.howItsDone: Catholics hear John 21 at Mass in the Easter season, and the Church reads Jesus's charge to Peter as part of the foundation of the papacy; feeding the hungry is one of the works of mercy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, breathed: Jesus in the locked room, receive ye the Holy Ghost. Your line was peace be to you. Were your first words peaceful? Day five hundred thirty-three.

Watch the fires in the last chapters of John. The night Jesus was arrested, Peter stood warming his hands at a charcoal fire in the high priest's courtyard and said three times, I don't know him. Now it's dawn on the shore of the Sea of Galilee. The disciples have been fishing all night. And on the beach, Jesus has made breakfast, fish and bread, cooking over a charcoal fire. John uses the same word, charcoal fire, for both. Peter can hardly miss it.
screen: `A CHARCOAL FIRE, THAT NIGHT.` → `I DON'T KNOW HIM, THREE TIMES.` → `ANOTHER CHARCOAL FIRE, AT DAWN.`

segments.voice: After they've eaten, Jesus turns to Peter. Simon son of John, lovest thou me more than these? Yes, Lord, you know I love you. Feed my lambs. Again: lovest thou me? Yes, Lord. Tend my sheep. And a third time. John says Peter was grieved, because he asked the third time. Three denials, three questions. Peter answers, in the Douay-Rheims: "Lord, thou knowest all things: thou knowest that I love thee." And Jesus says: "Feed my sheep." Notice what Jesus doesn't do. He doesn't make Peter explain the denials or promise never to fail again. He asks one question, about love, and then hands him work. Each yes becomes a job. In Greek, Jesus uses two different verbs for love, and Peter answers with one of them; scholars still debate how much weight to give that. What isn't debated is the pattern: the man who failed three times is restored three times, by the same fire. Catholics see here Peter given the care of the whole flock, part of the foundation of the Pope's office as the shepherd of the Church. Then John ends his Gospel with a shrug of wonder. Jesus did many other things, he says, and if they were all written down, he supposes the world itself couldn't contain the books. That closes six weeks in John: the Word made flesh, water into wine, Nicodemus at night, the woman at the well, the bread of life, golden lampstands, the good shepherd, Lazarus, the towel, the vine, the cross, and Mary in the garden. Tomorrow, the story keeps going in a second book.
screen: `THREE QUESTIONS AT DAWN.` · `EACH YES BECOMES A JOB.` · `PETER, SHEPHERD OF THE FLOCK.` · `THE WORLD COULDN'T HOLD THE BOOKS.` · then, large: `FEED MY SHEEP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan to feed someone. Sit and breathe. Picture a table, or a kitchen counter, or a bag of groceries. Who in your life could use a meal today? A neighbor, a coworker eating lunch alone, someone grieving, a kid, a stranger outside the store. Let one person come clearly to mind, and decide what you'll actually give them. If you pray, you can hold Peter's answer, Lord, thou knowest that I love thee, and let the meal be how you say it. If you don't, just hold the person. The bell holds the time.
Charcoal fire. The same word John uses for Peter's denial and for the breakfast fire where Jesus restores him with three questions about love. Today's word.
Your line: each yes becomes a job. Today, turn one yes into something you actually do for someone, quietly. Day five hundred thirty-three.

534.title: To the ends of the earth (Acts 1:6–8)
534.hook: you shall receive power and be witnesses
534.howItsDone: Catholics hear Acts 1:1–11 on the Solemnity of the Ascension, forty days after Easter (moved to the following Sunday in many places), and Acts is read at weekday and Sunday Masses through the Easter season.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the end of John: three questions on the beach, by a charcoal fire. Your line was each yes becomes a job. What did you turn into action? Day five hundred thirty-four.

Some stories get a sequel. Luke's does. His Gospel finishes with Jesus blessing the disciples and being carried up into heaven. Then he writes a second volume, addressed to the same reader, someone called Theophilus, and opens it by saying, in my first book I told you what Jesus began to do and to teach. Began. Everything so far was the beginning. Today we start that second book, the Acts of the Apostles. It opens on a hill outside Jerusalem, with the disciples asking the wrong question.
screen: `A SEQUEL, PROMISED.` → `WHAT JESUS BEGAN TO DO.` → `THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES.`

segments.voice: For forty days after the resurrection, Luke says, Jesus has been appearing to them and speaking about the kingdom of God. Now they ask: Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel? It's an understandable question. They want to know when, and they want it to look like what they expected. Jesus doesn't argue. He says the times aren't theirs to know. And then he gives them something else, in the Douay-Rheims: "But you shall receive the power of the Holy Ghost coming upon you, and you shall be witnesses unto me in Jerusalem, and in all Judea, and Samaria, and even to the uttermost part of the earth." Then he's lifted up and a cloud takes him out of their sight. That one sentence is a map of the whole book. Acts starts in Jerusalem, moves out into Judea and Samaria, and ends with Paul preaching in Rome, the empire's capital. And the word to hold is witness. In Greek it's martys. A witness, in a courtroom, is someone who says what they saw. Not an expert, not a salesman, just someone who was there. In time, Christians used the same word for those who died rather than deny what they'd seen: martyr. The Catechism calls martyrdom the supreme witness. But here Jesus doesn't tell them to die. He tells them who they'll be: people whose lives tell what they've seen. Not you shall do witnessing, but you shall be witnesses. It's a description, not a task list.
screen: `WILL YOU RESTORE THE KINGDOM NOW?` · `JERUSALEM TO THE ENDS OF THE EARTH.` · `MARTYS: ONE WHO SAW.` · `NOT DO WITNESSING: BE WITNESSES.` · then, large: `WITNESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think about what your life shows. Sit and breathe. Picture yourself from the outside, the way a coworker or a neighbor or a kid sees you on an ordinary day. What would they say you care about, just from watching? Not from what you say. From what you do. No judging, just noticing. Then pick one small thing you'd like them to see today: patience in a line, honesty about a mistake, a kindness. If you pray, you can hold the line, you shall be witnesses unto me. If you don't, just hold the picture. The bell holds the time.
Witness. In Greek, martys: someone who tells what they saw, and later, someone who gave their life for it. Today's word.
Your line: you shall be witnesses. Today, be a quiet witness: let your one small thing be seen, without saying a word about it. Day five hundred thirty-four.

535.title: Matthias (Acts 1:15–26)
535.hook: they pray, cast lots, and the twelfth place is filled
535.howItsDone: Catholics keep a feast of Saint Matthias, Apostle, and the Church often begins important choices, like a papal conclave, with a Mass asking the Holy Spirit's guidance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the start of Acts, and the word witness. Your line was you shall be witnesses. What did your day quietly show? Day five hundred thirty-five.

Every team photo with an empty spot has a story. A chair left empty at the table, a name missing from the roster. Someone has to decide whether to fill it, and how. After the Ascension the disciples go back to an upper room in Jerusalem and pray together, about a hundred and twenty of them, Luke says, with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus. There were twelve apostles. Now there are eleven. And Peter, only weeks after his own worst failure, stands up to deal with the empty chair.
screen: `AN EMPTY CHAIR.` → `A HUNDRED AND TWENTY IN PRAYER.` → `TWELVE, NOW ELEVEN.`

segments.voice: Peter speaks about Judas plainly and without gloating: he was numbered with us and had a share in this ministry. Then he gives the qualifications for the empty place. It has to be someone who was with them the whole time, from John's baptism to the day Jesus was taken up, someone who can be a witness with them of the resurrection. That's yesterday's word, witness, as the job description. Two men fit: Joseph called Barsabas, also known as Justus, and Matthias. Both, we're told, were there from the start, and Acts tells us nothing more about either one. Then they do two things, in this order. First they pray, saying: Lord, you who know the hearts of all, show which of these two you have chosen. And then they cast lots, something like drawing straws. In the Douay-Rheims: "And they gave them lots, and the lot fell upon Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles." Casting lots was an old way in Israel of leaving a decision to God; Proverbs says the lot is cast, but the decision is the Lord's. Some readers notice that once the Spirit comes at Pentecost, Acts shows the apostles deciding in other ways, by prayer, discussion and the Spirit's lead. What stays is the order: they prayed first. And Matthias, chosen by a falling lot, is honored by the Church as an apostle. Faithful from the beginning, and Acts never names him again.
screen: `THE EMPTY PLACE.` · `A WITNESS FROM THE START.` · `THEY PRAY, THEN CAST LOTS.` · `CHOSEN, THEN NEVER NAMED AGAIN.` · then, large: `MATTHIAS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray before a choice. Sit and breathe. Bring to mind a decision in front of you, large or small: a job, a conversation, a purchase, where to spend Saturday. Hold the options side by side, the way the apostles held two names. Don't decide yet. Just let them sit there together while you breathe. If you pray, you can borrow the apostles' request in your own words, asking God, who knows the heart, to show you. If you don't, simply hold the options in quiet before you choose. The bell holds the time.
Matthias. Chosen after prayer and the casting of lots to take the twelfth place among the apostles. Today's word.
Your line: they prayed first. Today, before one decision, even a small one, stop for a single breath before you choose. Day five hundred thirty-five.

536.title: Peter's first sermon (Acts 2:14–41)
536.hook: the man who denied him now preaches, and three thousand are baptized
536.tomorrow: Silver and gold I have none
536.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate Pentecost at the close of the Easter season, reading Acts 2 at Mass, and the Church often calls the day its birthday; adults are often received into the Church at Easter after a period of preparation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Matthias, chosen for the empty place. Your line was they prayed first. Did you pause before a choice? Day five hundred thirty-six.

Not long ago, a servant girl in a courtyard asked Peter a simple question, aren't you one of his? And he said he wasn't. Now it's the feast of Pentecost, and Jerusalem is full of devout pilgrims, Luke says, from every nation under heaven. The disciples have just poured out of a house, filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking in languages they never learned, and a crowd has gathered to stare. Some people laugh: they're drunk. And the man who stands up to answer them is Peter.
screen: `A SERVANT GIRL'S QUESTION.` → `PENTECOST, THE CITY PACKED.` → `PETER STANDS UP.`

segments.voice: His opening line is almost a joke. These men aren't drunk, as you suppose; it's only the third hour of the day, nine in the morning. Then he gets serious. He quotes the prophet Joel: in the last days, God says, I will pour out my spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, young men shall see visions, old men shall dream dreams. This, Peter says, is that. He tells them about Jesus of Nazareth, his miracles, his death, and that God raised him up, and we are all witnesses. There's that word witness again. He quotes the psalms of David, and ends on the claim that God has made this crucified Jesus both Lord and Christ. Luke says the listeners were cut to the heart. They ask, what shall we do? And Peter answers, in the Douay-Rheims: "Do penance, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ, for the remission of your sins: and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost." Do penance follows the Latin. The Greek word, metanoēsate, means change your mind, turn around, a whole new direction. That day, Luke says, about three thousand were added. And consider who's speaking. Not a polished speaker. A fisherman who, only weeks earlier, couldn't stand up to a servant girl. That courage didn't come from practice. Acts is clear about where it came from: the Spirit poured out that morning. The coward preached. And Catholics often call that feast the Church's birthday.
screen: `NOT DRUNK: IT'S NINE A.M.` · `JOEL: THIS IS THAT.` · `CUT TO THE HEART.` · `THREE THOUSAND, THAT DAY.` · then, large: `PETER'S FIRST SERMON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the place to speak up once. Sit and breathe. Think of a moment coming up today or this week where you usually stay quiet: a meeting, a family dinner, a friend saying something unkind, a chance to say what you believe. Picture yourself there. Picture opening your mouth and saying one true sentence, plainly and kindly. Feel your feet on the floor while you imagine it. If you pray, you can ask the Holy Spirit for the courage Peter was given. If you don't, simply rehearse the sentence. The bell holds the time.
Pentecost. The feast when Peter, the fisherman who once denied Jesus, stood up before the crowd, and about three thousand were baptized. Today's word.
Your line: the coward preached. Today, say your one true sentence when the moment comes, out loud and kindly. Day five hundred thirty-six.

537.title: Silver and gold I have none (Acts 3:1–10)
537.hook: but what I have, I give thee: rise and walk
537.howItsDone: Catholics are taught the corporal and spiritual works of mercy, giving not only money but time, care, counsel and prayer to people in need.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter's first sermon at Pentecost. Your line was the coward preached. Did you say your one true sentence? Day five hundred thirty-seven.

Most of us know the little calculation at a red light when someone with a cardboard sign walks between the cars. Do I have cash? Is the light about to change? Do I look, or do I keep my eyes on the dashboard? Usually the eyes win. Looking is the hard part. Afternoon in Jerusalem, three o'clock, the hour of prayer. Peter and John are walking up to the temple. At one of the gates, a man who has never walked in his life is being set down, the way he is every day, to ask for money.
screen: `THE RED-LIGHT CALCULATION.` → `THREE O'CLOCK, THE HOUR OF PRAYER.` → `A MAN AT THE GATE.`

segments.voice: Luke says he was lame from his mother's womb, carried every day to the gate of the temple called Beautiful, to beg from people going in. He sees Peter and John and asks for alms, the way he asks everyone. And then something unusual happens. Peter, with John, fixes his eyes on him and says, look at us. The man looks up, expecting a coin. And Peter says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Silver and gold I have none; but what I have, I give thee: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, arise, and walk." Peter takes him by the right hand and lifts him up, and the man's feet and ankles grow strong. He jumps up, stands, walks, and goes into the temple with them, walking and leaping and praising God. Everyone recognizes him. He's the one from the gate. Notice the order. First, eye contact: look at us. Before anything is given, the man is seen. Then an honest no: I don't have money. Then what Peter does have, which isn't his own. It's the name of Jesus. Peter's not pretending to be richer than he is, and he's not pretending to be poorer either. There's a story people tell about Thomas Aquinas visiting the pope while gold was being counted. The pope said, the Church can no longer say silver and gold I have none. And Thomas answered, no, and neither can she say, rise and walk. Nobody can confirm it happened. But it's stuck around for centuries because it names the temptation in today's line.
screen: `THE GATE CALLED BEAUTIFUL.` · `FIRST: LOOK AT US.` · `NO GOLD, BUT WHAT I HAVE.` · `AQUINAS AND THE COUNTED GOLD.` · then, large: `SILVER AND GOLD I HAVE NONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take stock of what you actually have. Sit, rest your hands open on your lap, and breathe. Not money, necessarily. What can you give today? Maybe time, a skill, a car with an empty seat, a listening ear, a language you speak, a kind word, your full attention. Name two or three things, quietly. Then picture one person who needs one of them. If you pray, you can hold Peter's words, what I have, I give thee, and offer it. If you don't, just keep your hands open. The bell holds the time.
Beautiful. The gate of the temple where a man who had never walked begged every day, until Peter said, what I have, I give thee: arise and walk. Today's word.
Your line: what I have I give. Today, look someone in the eye who usually gets looked past, and give them something you actually have. Day five hundred thirty-seven.

538.title: We cannot but speak (Acts 4:13–20)
538.hook: ordinary uneducated men astonish the council
538.howItsDone: Catholics read the Acts of the Apostles at Mass through the Easter season, and the Church keeps a feast for Catherine of Siena, a Doctor of the Church with little formal schooling.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the man at the Beautiful gate, and silver and gold I have none. Your line was what I have I give. Who did you really look at? Day five hundred thirty-eight.

A diploma on the wall tells you where someone studied. It can't tell you what they've seen. After the healing at the gate, Peter and John spent the night in custody. In the morning they're brought before the council: rulers, elders and scribes, men trained in the law of Moses. Facing them, two fishermen from Galilee. And next to the fishermen, on his own two feet, stands the man who used to beg at the gate. The council has a question for them.
screen: `A DIPLOMA ON THE WALL.` → `A NIGHT IN CUSTODY.` → `THE HEALED MAN STANDS WITH THEM.`

segments.voice: The council asks, by what power, by what name, have you done this? Peter answers: by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth. And then Luke describes the council's reaction. They saw the boldness of Peter and John, and realized they were unlettered, ordinary men, and they were amazed, and they recognized that these two had been with Jesus. Two words in the Greek are worth knowing. Agrammatoi: unlettered, not trained in the schools of the law. And idiōtai: ordinary people, private persons, not officials. English later got the word idiot from it, but here it just means laymen. The Douay calls their courage constancy. The Greek is parrēsia, freedom of speech, the boldness to say everything plainly. And the council can't say much back, Luke notes, because the healed man is standing right there. So they order the two to stop speaking or teaching in the name of Jesus at all. Peter and John answer: whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you judge. And then, in the Douay-Rheims: "For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard." Notice, it's not stubbornness, and it isn't a debating point. They simply can't un-see what they saw. It's the word from four days ago, witness, under pressure. And the reason given for their boldness isn't schooling. It's that they had been with Jesus. Catholics see the same pattern in some saints with little schooling. Catherine of Siena, tradition says, learned to write only late in life, and the Church later named her a Doctor of the Church.
screen: `BY WHAT NAME?` · `UNLETTERED, ORDINARY MEN.` · `THEY HAD BEEN WITH JESUS.` · `WHAT WE HAVE SEEN AND HEARD.` · then, large: `WE CANNOT BUT SPEAK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember what you've seen. Sit and breathe. Let your mind go back to one thing you've witnessed yourself that you can't un-see: an act of kindness that stopped you, a recovery, a forgiveness, a moment in prayer, something beautiful. Not something you read. Something you saw or heard. Let the details come back. Then think of who might need to hear about it. If you pray, you can give thanks for it, and hold the line, we cannot but speak. If you don't, just hold the memory. The bell holds the time.
Parrēsia. The Greek word for the boldness of two unlettered fishermen before the council, the courage that came from having been with Jesus. Today's word.
Your line: they had been with Jesus. Today, tell someone about something you've seen or experienced, plainly, without dressing it up. Day five hundred thirty-eight.

539.title: Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5:1–11)
539.hook: a hard story about lying to the community
539.carry: the bible keeps the hard stories
539.howItsDone: Catholics examine their conscience, often at night, and confess serious sins in the sacrament of penance; the early community's sharing in Acts 4 and 5 is read at Mass in the Easter season.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two ordinary men before the council. Your line was they had been with Jesus. What did you tell someone you'd seen? Day five hundred thirty-nine.

Founding stories tend to get polished. The brochure keeps the triumphs and quietly drops the rest. Which makes this part of Acts surprising. Luke has just described the first Christians in Jerusalem as one heart and one soul, sharing everything, so that no one among them was in need. A man named Barnabas sells a field and lays the money at the apostles' feet. And then, right after that glowing picture, Luke tells a story that is very hard to read.
screen: `THE STORY LEFT OUT.` → `ONE HEART AND ONE SOUL.` → `THEN, A HARD STORY.`

segments.voice: A married couple, Ananias and Sapphira, sell a piece of land too. They keep back part of the money and bring the rest, presenting it as the whole. Nobody required them to sell, or to give it all. Peter says so: while it remained, was it not yours? And after it was sold, wasn't the money in your power? The problem isn't the amount. It's the pretending. Peter tells Ananias: "Thou hast not lied to men, but to God." And Ananias falls down and dies. About three hours later Sapphira comes in, not knowing what has happened. Peter asks her straight: did you sell the land for so much? She says yes, for so much. And she falls down and dies too. Luke says great fear came upon the whole church: the Greek word is ekklēsia, the assembly. What do we do with a story like this? The text doesn't explain how they died or say anything about their eternal fate. Some readers see God's judgment; others see a shock so great it killed them; the passage itself doesn't settle it. What it does say is that a community built on sharing can be poisoned by pretending, by people performing generosity they don't have. And Luke didn't leave it out. The founding story of the Church includes this, and Peter's denial, and the disciples' squabbles. That's week seventy-seven: feed my sheep, witness, Matthias, Peter's first sermon, silver and gold, we cannot but speak, and a hard story. The Bible keeps the hard stories.
